# Four Blackwell Formats, One Model: Quantizing Qwen3-32B on RTX PRO 6000

Jaydev Tonde

AI Engineer

October 5, 2026· 20 min read

...

NVIDIA's Blackwell chips change that. ... What Blackwell adds is native FP4 (and FP6) math and hardware support for microscaling (MX) block formats, so 4-bit floating point runs natively instead of being faked in software. The lineup goes from the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition up to the data-center B200 / GB200 systems. This matters because on older hardware, quantization was mostly a way to make a model small enough to fit in memory — any speedup was a bonus, and usually a small one. On Blackwell, the low-bit formats run on dedicated hardware, so moving to FP8 or FP4 gives you real, measurable speed, not just less memory use.

...

The result is a fair, side-by-side comparison of BF16, FP8-AWQ, MXFP8-AWQ, NVFP4-AWQ, and MXFP4-AWQ on the same hardware — boiled down to three charts and one table you can act on. The rest of this post walks through both sides, starting with a short look at how the quantization works. For a deeper theoretical and hands-on introduction, see our earlier post, The vLLM Quantization Complete Guide + Benchmarks. It covers the well-known algorithms, including AWQ, GPTQ, BitsAndBytes, TorchAO, Marlin-AWQ, Marlin-GPTQ, BitBLAS and ModelOPT.

results.title: DeepInfer: What DeepSeek Open-Sourced, and What It Kept
results.author: Vishnu Subramanian
highlights:
DeepInfer: What DeepSeek Open-Sourced, and What It Kept

# DeepInfer: What DeepSeek Open-Sourced, and What It Kept

Vishnu Subramanian

Founder @ Jarvislabs

October 21, 2026· 12 min read

DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer yesterday. It is the inference engine behind their DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash API. According to DeepSeek, a single cluster running it serves 155 trillion tokens a day and earns about $38 per GPU-hour, and that's at off-peak prices. It's the same engine they run in production, released under Apache 2.0.

...

H100s, H200s, A100s and more — per-second billing, no commitments.

...

DeepSeek published an EP8 vs EP64 decode benchmark. I pulled two points from it and compared them per GPU, because per GPU is what you pay for.

| Scenario | Per-user speed | EP8 (tokens/s/GPU) | EP64 (tokens/s/GPU) | EP64 advantage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Batch, 256 requests per GPU | ~100 tokens/s | 24.9k | 26.3k | ~6% |
| Interactive | ~240 tokens/s | ~1.9k | ~15.7k | ~8x |

...

So you don't need 128 GPUs to get value from this. The big cluster is what you pay for fast responses. And since today's release only does offline inference, the 8-GPU batch case is the one most people can actually run.

...

Batch and interactive are different products. DeepSeek's own chart says an 8-GPU node gets about 94% of the per-GPU decode throughput of a 64-GPU group when nobody is waiting. The large scale-up domain is what you pay for responsiveness. That's a useful way to think about pricing batch versus real-time inference.

results.title: How a ComfyUI Workflow Works, and How to Run It From Python
results.author: Sanchit Jain
highlights:
# How a ComfyUI Workflow Works, and How to Run It From Python

Sanchit Jain

AI Engineer @ Jarvislabs

October 6, 2026· 10 min read

Open ComfyUI's LTX-2.3 template and you are looking at fifty nodes. Nine settings are yours to change, and the rest is wiring. This is how to tell them apart, and how to run the whole thing from Python once you want to.

...

The models. A workflow stores the names of the models it needs, not the models. Open the template on a fresh machine and ComfyUI lists what is missing before it will run anything.

Five files, 42.97 GB, most of it one 29 GB checkpoint. They land on your volume, so you pay this once.

On a Jarvislabs instance much of this is already cached, so there is nothing to download. In future that store will hold over a hundred models.

| File | Size | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ltx-2.3-22b-dev-fp8` | 29.15 GB | The main model. Turns noise into a picture and a soundtrack. |
| `gemma_3_12B_it_fp4_mixed` | 9.45 GB | Reads your prompt and turns it into something the model understands. |
| `ltx_2.3_22b_distilled_1.1_lora` | 2.74 GB | Makes it fast. Seconds instead of minutes. |
| `ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1` | 1.00 GB | Generates at half size and doubles it, which is cheaper than making it big from the start. |
| `gemma-3-12b-it-abliterated_lora` | 0.63 GB | Adjusts how the prompt is read. We did not test what it changes. |

Every node here ships with ComfyUI — no custom packs, nothing to install. The models are the opposite: downloaded once, then kept on your volume.

> Download lands on the GPU, not your browser. ComfyUI's missing-models dialog is an ordinary browser link, so on a rented machine it fetches tens of gigabytes to the wrong computer. On a Jarvislabs instance that fetch happens on the server instead.

...

The forty-two nodes you are ignoring are what those four lines actually do.

With the models already loaded, each video takes 14.38 seconds — about 1.6 cents at the H200 rate at Jarvislabs.

This is what came out of it: one photograph in, five seconds of video out.

The still we started from, and the five seconds it became. Play it with sound: the rain was generated in the same pass as the picture, from the same sentence. Nothing here was filmed or recorded.

There is no separate audio model and no separate audio step. The same model builds the picture and the sound together, in one pass, from the same sentence.

results.title: Wan 2.2 Lightning in ComfyUI: 85% faster, but a different video
results.author: Sanchit Jain
highlights:
# Wan 2.2 Lightning in ComfyUI: 85% faster, but a different video

Sanchit Jain

AI Engineer @ Jarvislabs

November 2, 2026· 10 min read

Lightning, the turbo switch in ComfyUI's Wan 2.2 text-to-video template, renders each clip 85% faster. In our copy of the template's graph on one NVIDIA H200, a 5-second 640×640 clip went from 151.8 to 22.4 seconds. But the same prompt and seed give you a different video, not a faster copy of the one you had.

results.title: Make Wan 2.2 render about 24% faster in ComfyUI: one setting, near-identical video
results.author: Sanchit Jain
highlights:
# Make Wan 2.2 render about 24% faster in ComfyUI: one setting, near-identical video

Sanchit Jain

AI Engineer @ Jarvislabs

October 8, 2026· 10 min read

In ComfyUI's Wan 2.2 text-to-video template, set the second sampler's cfg to 1.0 and leave the first alone. Each clip renders about 24% faster, with near-identical video. A sampler is the node that runs a model; its cfg value is how strongly the model is pushed toward your prompt.

On one NVIDIA H200, with the template as it ships on Jarvislabs, a 5-second 1280×720 clip went from 632 to 477 seconds. That is about 2.5 minutes back on every clip, or 4.3 hours over 100 clips.
